name: Julia
language: Julia (C/C++ runtime on LLVM; embeddable from C/C++ through libjulia)
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1, PyPy 3 (7.3.x), Node.js (V8) and OpenJDK HotSpot, on the same CPU-bound algorithms
workload: Single-threaded CPU-bound programs written with the same algorithm in every language: kostya/benchmarks brainfuck interpreter (bench.b, mandel.b) and naive matrix multiply; plb2 nqueen, matmul (1500x1500), sudoku, bedcov.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks), brainfuck bench.b: Julia 1.564 s vs Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s, Node.js 2.954 s (Java 1.191 s is faster than Julia); mandel.b: Julia 30.315 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s (Java 13.041 s faster); matmul without BLAS: Julia 1.113 s vs Java 3.057 s, Node.js 3.212 s, pypy 3.263 s. Ratios on bench.b: about 3.6x vs LuaJIT and 6.0x vs PyPy; about 2.7x vs OpenJDK on naive matmul (derived from page data). Second source, plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Apple M1): Julia 1.10.0 nqueen 3.02 s, matmul 0.76 s, sudoku 2.18 s, bedcov 1.96 s vs luajit 5.31/2.66/4.48/10.52 s, PyPy 7.3.14 6.91/4.89/8.82/6.27 s, Java 3.92/1.14/3.20/3.04 s, Node 3.73/2.88/3.77/2.45 s.
compiler_and_flags: kostya/benchmarks: julia v1.11.6 run as `julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no`; Java 24.0.2, Node.js v26.5.0, luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23 (Python 3.11.15), Docker on Debian; run commands in common/commands.mk. plb2 versions in its README table (Julia 1.10.0, Java 20.0.1, PyPy 7.3.14, LuaJIT 2.1, Node 21.5.0).
hardware: kostya/benchmarks: Intel Xeon E-2324G; plb2: Apple M1 MacBook Pro
tradeoffs: Per-process JIT warmup and large footprint (kostya bench.b base RSS about 244 MB vs 2.5 MB for LuaJIT); package precompilation latency; garbage collected; embedding in C++ goes through the libjulia C API and is heavier than embedding LuaJIT.
caveats: Java beats Julia on kostya's bench.b and mandel.b, and in kostya's other tests Julia loses to the baselines (base64 3.085 s vs Node.js 0.635 s and PyPy 3.534 s; primes 0.680 s vs luajit 0.309 s, Node.js 0.207 s and PyPy 0.617 s; JSON3 0.700 s vs PyPy 0.606 s), so the win is workload specific: numeric loops yes, string and allocation-heavy work no. In plb2 Julia beats all four baselines. The kostya run uses --check-bounds=no (bounds checks removed) and plb2's Julia sources use @inbounds in the hot loops, which other languages' sources do not. Julia matmul 0.12-0.17 s rows use BLAS and are not comparable; only 'no BLAS' is a like-for-like loop. kostya times exclude data loading; whether Julia JIT compile time is inside the timed region was not checked.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'JIT benchmark comparison LuaJIT PyPy V8 HotSpot GraalVM results ...' led to the attractivechaos/plb2 and kostya/benchmarks READMEs; Julia rows read from both tables

name: Codon
language: C++ (compiler for a Python-syntax language, LLVM based)
workload: Benchmarks-game style single-threaded programs (binarytrees, brainfuck, fasta, knucleotide, matmul, nbody, spectralnorm, ...) written as ordinary Python and built with `codon build --release`; timing is measured inside the program, so compile time is reported in a separate column.
claimed_speedup: kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (https://github.com/kostya/jit-benchmarks), best time in s, Codon vs PyPy3: binarytrees 1.0 vs 3.84, brainfuck 2.05 vs 8.77, brainfuck2 1.91 vs 11.03, fasta 1.66 vs 3.19, knucleotide 2.69 vs 3.7, matmul 0.25 vs 0.36, nbody 2.23 vs 4.44, spectralnorm 0.53 vs 0.71. Against LuaJIT: binarytrees 1.0 vs 6.73, brainfuck2 1.91 vs 8.32, fasta 1.66 vs 1.71, matmul 0.25 vs 0.27. Slower than PyPy on fannkuchredux (1.82 vs 0.71) and mandelbrot (0.65 vs 0.54), slower than LuaJIT on knucleotide (2.69 vs 0.77), and no result ('-') for pidigits, regexdna, revcomp. Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Apple M1, Codon 0.18.0): nqueen 2.82 s, matmul 2.49 s, sudoku 3.08 s vs PyPy 7.3.14 6.91, 4.89, 8.82 s.
compiler_and_flags: codon 0.15.5 built with `codon build --release -o out source` (kostya tools/languages.rb); pypy3 7.3.11 (gcc 10.2.1); luajit 2.1.0-beta3; Docker on Ubuntu 22.10. plb2 uses `codon build -release -exe`.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4 3200 MHz (as written in the README); plb2: Apple M1
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler, not a tracing JIT: it needs static type inference and supports a Python subset (no full dynamic semantics, some stdlib and C-extension interop only through a Python bridge); 4-5 s compile time per program in the kostya table; produces native binaries callable from C/C++ with effort.
caveats: Results are from February 2023 (Codon 0.15.5 vs PyPy 7.3.11); compile time is excluded from 'Best T' (for example 4.28 s on binarytrees); three tests did not run; mixed on fannkuchredux and mandelbrot. The repo README itself only compares with CPython (65x on fib(40)), the PyPy comparison comes from the third-party suites.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'JIT benchmark comparison LuaJIT PyPy V8 HotSpot GraalVM results ...' surfaced kostya/jit-benchmarks; plb2 README table lists the codon row

name: LuaJIT Remake (Deegen)
workload: Lua 5.1 benchmark programs in the repo's luabench directory, geometric mean over all benchmarks, each repeated 5 times, with GC turned off in all implementations.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter is 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter and 185% faster than the official PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (geometric mean, README).
compiler_and_flags: Built in Docker with `python3 ljr-build make release`; compiler flags and the LuaJIT/PUC Lua build options are not stated in the README.
tradeoffs: x86-64 Linux only; no garbage collector yet; some standard library missing (require and module); Lua 5.1 only; the multi-tier JIT is unfinished, so only the generated interpreter is a usable result; interpreter and JIT are generated from bytecode semantics descriptions (Deegen).
caveats: Compares interpreters only: LuaJIT's own JIT, which is the reason to use LuaJIT, is not the baseline, so this does not show a faster JIT. GC disabled for fair comparison. Benchmark flags and per-benchmark numbers are only in a PNG figure. The Deegen paper (arXiv 2411.11469) and the author's blog posts were not opened (hosts blocked). Last commit February 2025.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'Lua implementation faster than LuaJIT benchmark interpreter JIT github' (project README)

name: .NET runtime (CoreCLR RyuJIT)
baseline: OpenJDK HotSpot (Java 20.0.1), LuaJIT 2.1 and PyPy 7.3.14, on the plb2 tasks
workload: plb2 single-threaded CPU-bound tasks with the same algorithm in each language: nqueen (15 queens), matmul (1500x1500), sudoku (4000 puzzles), bedcov (1M intervals).
claimed_speedup: plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2) table, seconds, .NET 8.0.100: nqueen 2.82, matmul 1.38, sudoku 1.62, bedcov 0.99 vs OpenJDK 20.0.1 3.92, 1.14, 3.20, 3.04 (faster on 3 of 4); vs luajit 5.31, 2.66, 4.48, 10.52 and PyPy 7.3.14 6.91, 4.89, 8.82, 6.27 (faster on all 4).
compiler_and_flags: C# built with `dotnet publish -c Release -r osx-arm64` (src/csharp/Makefile); runtime flags for Java, LuaJIT and PyPy are not given in the README.
tradeoffs: Large managed runtime; use from C++ goes through the hosting API (nethost/hostfxr) or Native AOT libraries; tiered JIT with warmup.
caveats: Mixed against HotSpot: slower on matmul in plb2 (1.38 vs 1.14 s). In kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks, Xeon E-2324G, .NET 10 vs Java 24.0.2) C#/.NET Core is slower than Java on bench.b (1.280 vs 1.191 s), mandel.b (15.576 vs 13.041 s), base64 (2.374 vs 1.435 s) and matmul (4.506 vs 3.057 s) and slower than PyPy on matmul (4.506 vs 3.263 s), though faster than LuaJIT (5.686 s) and PyPy (9.398 s) on bench.b. plb2 marks the .NET row with the AOT star although the Makefile shows a plain publish, so the mode is unclear. The plb2 author notes that, being mostly a C programmer, his implementations in other languages may be suboptimal.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'JIT benchmark comparison LuaJIT PyPy V8 HotSpot GraalVM results ...' led to the plb2 README table; cross-checked against kostya/benchmarks tables

name: Dart SDK (Dart VM)
language: Dart and C++ (the SDK includes the VM)
workload: plb2 single-threaded CPU-bound tasks: nqueen (15 queens), matmul (1500x1500), sudoku, bedcov.
claimed_speedup: plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2) row 'dart:jit' (Dart 3.2.4), seconds: nqueen 3.62, matmul 2.74, sudoku 3.24, bedcov 2.85 vs PyPy 6.91, 4.89, 8.82, 6.27 (faster on all 4); vs luajit 5.31, 2.66, 4.48, 10.52 (faster on 3 of 4, matmul slightly slower); vs OpenJDK 20.0.1 3.92, 1.14, 3.20, 3.04 (faster on nqueen and bedcov, slower on matmul, about equal on sudoku).
compiler_and_flags: Dart 3.2.4; the plb2 src/dart/Makefile builds with `dart compile exe` (AOT); run mode for the 'dart:jit' row is not stated.
tradeoffs: Dart VM is a full language runtime with its own object model and GC; embedding from C++ is possible through the Dart embedding API but is niche; JIT startup warmup.
caveats: Label says JIT but the Makefile compiles AOT executables, so it is not certain which mode was timed. Win over HotSpot is narrow and mixed. Benchmarks measure one author's ports of four small programs. plb2 was last updated January 2025 (Codon bump); the Dart numbers date from the Dec 2023 / Jan 2024 run.

name: Graal.js (GraalJS)
workload: Are We Fast Yet suite (CD, DeltaBlue, Havlak, Json, Richards, Bounce, List, Mandelbrot, NBody, Permute, Queens, Sieve, Storage, Towers) after warmup, peak performance, runtime normalised to Java 1.8.0_91.
claimed_speedup: Are We Fast Yet performance report (https://github.com/smarr/are-we-fast-yet/blob/master/docs/performance.md) runtime factor over Java, geomean: Graal.js 2.23 (median 2.13, sd 2.82) vs Node.js 2.89 (median 2.54, sd 3.33), i.e. about 1.3x lower geomean runtime than Node.js (derived from page data). Maxima are equal (12.22 vs 12.25).
compiler_and_flags: Java 1.8.0_91 baseline; Graal.js and Node.js versions and flags are not stated on the page (report generated 2016-06-20).
tradeoffs: Runs on the JVM (Java and Truffle/Graal compiler); long warmup and high memory; native-image distribution exists; Java interoperability; JavaScript only, no V8 embedding API from C++.
caveats: Numbers are from June 2016 (published suite from the DLS'16 paper by Marr, Daloze and Mössenböck) and early Graal.js; current versions on both sides are unmeasured here. Peak performance only, after warmup; startup not measured. Some benchmarks favour Node.js; the page's CPU is not stated. The community distribution is UPL-1.0 but Oracle's non-community builds are under the GraalVM Free Terms and Conditions.

name: TruffleRuby
language: Java (Ruby implementation on Truffle/Graal; C and C++ for extensions)
baseline: Node.js (V8) on Are We Fast Yet; LuaJIT 2.1 and PyPy 3 on kostya/benchmarks bench.b
workload: Are We Fast Yet suite after warmup (runtime factor over Java 1.8.0_91), and kostya/benchmarks brainfuck bench.b.
claimed_speedup: Are We Fast Yet (https://github.com/smarr/are-we-fast-yet/blob/master/docs/performance.md) geomean runtime factor over Java for 'JRuby+Truffle' (the predecessor name of TruffleRuby): 2.36 (sd 0.94, median 2.64) vs Node.js 2.89 (sd 3.33, median 2.54) and vs JRuby 12.83 and MRI 45.62; Node.js has the better median. Second source, kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks) bench.b: truffleruby 34.0.1 native 5.169 s and JVM mode 4.645 s vs Lua/luajit 5.686 s and Python/pypy 9.398 s (Node.js 2.954 s is faster).
compiler_and_flags: AWFY: Java 1.8.0_91 baseline, JRuby+Truffle version not stated (2016). kostya: truffleruby 34.0.1 run as `truffleruby` and `truffleruby-jvm-bin`, luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23.
hardware: AWFY page: not stated; kostya/benchmarks: Intel Xeon E-2324G
tradeoffs: Needs a lot of warmup and memory (kostya matmul RSS about 500 MB extra); JVM or native-image build; Ruby only; supports many C extensions; no GIL.
caveats: Mixed: kostya mandel.b 48.381 s vs luajit 31.804 s and matmul 17.776 s vs PyPy 3.263 s (slower), Node.js beats it on bench.b. AWFY numbers date from 2016. plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2) also lists Ruby on 'Graal EE 23.1.1' (nqueen 6.54, matmul 4.10, sudoku 4.11, bedcov 5.23 s vs PyPy 6.91/4.89/8.82/6.27) but that is the proprietary Enterprise build. The README claim ('fastest Ruby implementation', yjit-bench) compares against other Rubies, not the listed baselines.

name: Eclipse OpenJ9
workload: DayTrader 3 (stock trading web app) on OpenLiberty: startup time, memory footprint during ramp-up and after startup, and throughput over time.
claimed_speedup: openj9-website benchmark page (https://github.com/eclipse-openj9/openj9-website/blob/master/benchmark/daytrader3.md): with AOT, startup almost 40% faster than HotSpot, almost 50% faster with -Xquickstart; footprint about 60% smaller after startup and about 80% smaller during ramp-up; both reach similar peak throughput but OpenJ9 reaches it about 7 minutes sooner; CPU-constrained cloud scenario with -Xtune:virtualized 4x faster ramp-up.
compiler_and_flags: OpenJDK 9 with OpenJ9 (20170925 build) vs OpenJDK 9 with HotSpot (20172509 build); AOT runs used -Xshareclasses -Xscmx60M -Xscmaxaot8M; cloud runs -Xscmx150M -Xscmaxaot120m -Xtune:virtualized.
tradeoffs: Shared class cache and AOT code needed for the startup win; peak throughput is only on par with HotSpot; lower footprint; not every OpenJDK feature or tuning flag is identical.
caveats: First-party (IBM/Eclipse) numbers on JDK 9 from 2017; default OpenJ9 startup without AOT was slightly slower than HotSpot; the claim is startup and footprint, not peak throughput. Newer pages in the same directory (daytrader7.md, openjdk11-daytrader7.md, quarkus.md) were listed but not opened. The repository README itself carries no numbers. License shown on the repo page as dual EPL-2.0 and Apache-2.0.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'OpenJ9 vs HotSpot startup time footprint benchmark results throughput' (eclipse.dev pages blocked; opened the same page in openj9-website on github.com)

name: pg_jitter
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit); also PostgreSQL's expression interpreter
workload: PostgreSQL 18.1 queries on 1M-row tables (aggregation, joins, wide rows, text, numeric, jsonb), JIT thresholds set to 0, median of 3 timed runs after 2 warmups, parallel workers off.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md): SUM_int no JIT 44.859 ms, llvmjit 68.090 ms, sljit 42.401 ms, asmjit 42.201 ms, mir 45.620 ms; GroupBy_5agg no JIT 117.367 ms, llvmjit 149.033 ms, sljit 99.530 ms, asmjit 98.079 ms, mir 125.102 ms. README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): compile time 'tens to low hundreds of microseconds' (sljit) and 'hundreds of microseconds' (AsmJit) vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; average speedup over the interpreter TPC-C 8%, TPC-H 6%, ecommerce 14%, OLAP 42%, CRM ~400%.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; build flags for pg_jitter and PostgreSQL not stated on the page.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM, Darwin 25.2.0 arm64
tradeoffs: PostgreSQL extension only; beta quality by its own README; jit_above_cost must be lowered from 100000 to about 200-2000; avoid for point lookups; AsmJit backend only on arm64 and x86_64; adds embedded JIT libraries (sljit, AsmJit, MIR) in place of LLVM.
caveats: First-party benchmarks, one machine, ARM64 only (x86_64 results marked TBD); thresholds forced to 0 so LLVM compile cost is paid on every query, which favours the lightweight backends; per-query gains over the interpreter are small (README: sljit 5-25%); CRM benchmark is synthetic and built to show the strongest cases. The baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not one of the category baselines.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'asmjit benchmark code generation speed compared LLVM xbyak sljit JIT assembler performance' surfaced vladich/pg_jitter

name: sljit
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit) in the pg_jitter shootout
workload: Machine-code generation for PostgreSQL expression evaluation through the pg_jitter sljit backend (PostgreSQL 18.1, 1M-row tables, thresholds forced to 0).
claimed_speedup: pg_jitter README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): sljit compile 'tens to low hundreds of microseconds' vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md): SUM_int llvmjit 68.090 ms vs sljit 42.401 ms, GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 149.033 ms vs sljit 99.530 ms; README calls sljit 'the most consistent: 5-25% faster than the interpreter across all workloads'.
tradeoffs: Low-level stack-less JIT with a platform-independent API (x86, ARM, RISC-V, s390x, PowerPC, LoongArch, MIPS); you write the code generator yourself (no optimizer); used by PCRE2.
caveats: Indirect evidence: the numbers measure pg_jitter's sljit backend, not the library alone, and the sljit repo page has no benchmark of its own. Baseline is LLVM as used by PostgreSQL, not a listed baseline. Same first-party, ARM64-only caveats as pg_jitter.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'asmjit benchmark code generation speed compared LLVM xbyak sljit JIT assembler performance' surfaced pg_jitter, which names sljit as its fastest backend

name: AsmJit
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit) in the pg_jitter shootout
workload: Machine-code generation for PostgreSQL expression evaluation through the pg_jitter AsmJit backend (PostgreSQL 18.1, 1M-row tables, thresholds forced to 0).
claimed_speedup: pg_jitter README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): AsmJit compile 'hundreds of microseconds' vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; 'AsmJIT excels on wide-row/deform-heavy queries (up to 32% faster)'; benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md): SUM_int llvmjit 68.090 ms vs asmjit 42.201 ms, GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 149.033 ms vs asmjit 98.079 ms.
tradeoffs: Assembler-level C++ API for x86, x86-64, AArch32 and AArch64 with a register allocator in the Compiler layer; no mid-level optimizer; the pg_jitter AsmJit backend supports only arm64 and x86_64.
caveats: Indirect evidence: numbers measure pg_jitter's AsmJit backend, and the AsmJit repo page carries no benchmark against LLVM. Baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not a listed baseline. First-party, ARM64-only caveats of pg_jitter apply.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'asmjit benchmark code generation speed compared LLVM xbyak sljit JIT assembler performance' surfaced pg_jitter, which uses AsmJit as a backend

name: Chez Scheme
workload: kostya/benchmarks brainfuck interpreter (bench.b and mandel.b); plb2 nqueen and matmul.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks), Chez Scheme 10.0.0: bench.b 1.758 s vs Node.js 2.954 s, Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s (Java 1.191 s is faster); mandel.b 30.884 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s (Java 13.041 s faster). Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Chez 9.5.8, Apple M1): nqueen 3.54 s vs luajit 5.31 s, PyPy 6.91 s and Node 3.73 s, but matmul 18.98 s vs 2.66 s (luajit) and 4.89 s (PyPy).
compiler_and_flags: kostya: `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program`, Chez Scheme 10.0.0 (optimize-level 3 is the unsafe level); luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23, Node.js v26.5.0, Java 24.0.2.
tradeoffs: Incremental native-code compiler with a Scheme runtime, not a general-purpose embeddable JIT; C interface exists; optimize-level 3 removes safety checks.
caveats: Mixed results: plb2 matmul is far slower than every JIT in the table, and Java beats Chez on both kostya brainfuck tests. Mode of execution (compile vs interpret of the program) was not checked; Chez compiles by default. Brainfuck programs are the only kostya test it appears in among the ones read.

name: R8 (NoClip, Rust V8)
workload: 12 workloads from the js-engines-benchmark suite (arithmetic loops, recursion, object operations, memory, arrays, strings, cryptography, algorithms, WebSockets, databases, HTTP routing, package resolution).
claimed_speedup: js-engines-benchmark README (https://github.com/NoClip/js-engines-benchmark): R8 '3.08x faster overall' than Google V8 TurboFan across 12 benchmarks (suite total 19.43 ms vs 59.82 ms), individual speedups from 1.38x (arithmetic) to 11.13x (HTTP routing).
tradeoffs: Described as a pure-Rust engine 'based on Google V8 version 12.8'; no C++ API; extremely young (first visible commit 2026-09-14, about 20-27 commits).
caveats: Very low confidence. Same author runs the engine and the benchmark repo; hardware, date and flags are not stated; each workload takes only a few milliseconds; the benchmark repo has a commit about preserving upstream function names and verifying honest execution 'without R8 cheats', which suggests harness-gaming concerns; the r8 README table (arithmetic loops 4.13 ms vs V8 7.82 ms) does not match the 1.38x figure on the benchmark repo page. A from-scratch Rust reimplementation of V8 that beats V8 TurboFan 3x in a month is not credible without independent reproduction. Included so the verifier can check the harness; expect rejection if the benchmark is invalid.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'JavaScript engine faster than V8 benchmark github open source JIT Octane Speedometer results' surfaced NoClip/js-engines-benchmark
